## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="b3-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Reading sequence</dt><dd>Sets, parameters, variables, objective, constraints: what is counted, given, chosen, scored and ruled out.</dd>
<dt>Indices and sums</dt><dd>p with indices g and t is a table; Σ over g adds a column, Σ over t a row.</dd>
<dt>Units</dt><dd>$/MWh × MW × h = $: every term of the objective in dollars, with Δt written out.</dd>
<dt>For all</dt><dd>One line with ∀ t ∈ T stands for one row per hour.</dd>
<dt>Verification</dt><dd>Does the model do what its equations say? Units, signs, balance, duals, a hand check.</dd>
<dt>Validation</dt><dd>Is the model right enough for the question? Compare with real data and expert judgement.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Why the balance dual is $0 at 17:00 and $80 at 18:00</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

A [balance dual]{.lx-term term="shadow-price"} is the change in the cheapest total cost when one hour's demand rises by 1 MWh. At 19:00 and 20:00 the combined-cycle plant simply makes 1 MW more: \$40.

At 18:00 it cannot. It already climbs its full 40 MW from 17:00 to 18:00, so one more MW at 18:00 means one more MW at 17:00 too, where nobody needs it and it pushes out free wind: \$40 + \$40 = \$80, still cheaper than the \$100 peaker.

At 17:00 the plan already spills 10 MW of wind and sun to warm the combined-cycle plant up for the evening. One more MWh of demand there just spills less: \$0. The hours are linked through the ramp, so the prices are too; the Modeler lesson M1 reads such duals as marginal values for a whole day.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>The same model in Pyomo</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

Each line of the formulation becomes one line of code, with the sets doing the copying. In [Pyomo](https://www.pyomo.org/), with `c`, `d`, `V` and `dt` holding the parameters:

```python
from pyomo.environ import *
m = ConcreteModel()
m.T = Set(initialize=[17, 18, 19, 20])
m.G = Set(initialize=["nuc", "wind", "solar", "cc", "pk"])
m.p = Var(m.G, m.T, within=NonNegativeReals)   # MW
m.u = Var(m.T, within=NonNegativeReals)        # MW
m.cost = Objective(expr=sum(c[g] * m.p[g, t] * dt for g in m.G for t in m.T)
                        + sum(V * m.u[t] * dt for t in m.T))
m.balance = Constraint(m.T, rule=lambda m, t:
    sum(m.p[g, t] for g in m.G) + m.u[t] == d[t])
```

Delete `m.T` from the balance and you have suspect 3; drop `* dt` and the objective is right only at one-hour steps. Reading code against the formulation, line by line, is the same skill as this lesson.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Researcher</span>Validation in published energy studies</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

Validating an optimization model is hard because it describes what would be cheapest, not what will happen. One test is to look back: for the UK's electricity transition from 1990 to 2014, the cumulative cost of the real path deviated by 9 to 23% from the cost-optimal paths of a model, under the study's alternative assumptions ([Trutnevyte, 2016](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.energy.2016.03.038)). Published guidance on good practice for energy-system optimization studies ([DeCarolis et al., 2017](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apenergy.2017.03.001)) asks for documented, verifiable models and for uncertainty to be explored rather than hidden. The Researcher lesson R5 (upcoming) turns both into a routine.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="b3-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="optimal" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A model that solves to ‘optimal’ has passed verification.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. All five suspects solved to optimal. The solver checks the mathematics, not whether it says what you meant.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="neg" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “In this model, a negative balance dual would be a warning sign.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. With spilling free, more demand can never make the cheapest plan cheaper. Real markets do see negative prices when output cannot be cut cheaply, so the expected sign depends on the model.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="dt" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Adding up p in MW over the hours gives energy in MWh.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Multiply by Δt first. With one-hour steps the number happens to be the same; at 15-minute steps the plain sum is four times too big.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="b3">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="fast" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">A model's cost is far below your hand estimate, and the dearest plant runs first. Which check finds the bug fastest?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">The units of every parameter</li><li data-value="b">The balance in every hour</li><li data-value="c">Counting rows</li><li data-value="d">The signs of the duals</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>The units: a cost in $/kWh read as $/MWh makes a plant look a thousand times cheaper, as suspect 1 showed. The balance still holds.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="rows" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">How many rows does p(g,t) ≤ P̄(g) ∀ g ∈ G, t ∈ T stand for, with 5 plants and a whole day of 24 hours?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">5</li><li data-value="b">24</li><li data-value="c">120</li><li data-value="d">29</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>120: one row for each plant in each hour, 5 × 24.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
</div>
```
